title: Aerolite 103 (Kawasaki 340 swap) — Normal and Emergency Procedures
description: A worked example of the case this corpus exists for: the same airframe as the baseline file, with a different engine, and a checklist that had to change because of it. Forked from aerolite-103-hirth-f33 and edited where the twin-cylinder Kawasaki installation forced a different procedure. AUTHORED, NOT TRANSCRIBED, and NOT AIRWORTHY: every number is a placeholder and no item has been checked against an aircraft. It is here to demonstrate lineage, not to be flown.

modifications.description: Hirth F-33 single cylinder replaced with a Kawasaki 340 twin. Both are published options for this airframe, but the twin has two carburettors, a different warm-up behaviour and a different static RPM, so the start and pre-takeoff sections are not interchangeable.
modifications.reference: Manufacturer specification page lists both engine options for the type.

modifications.description: Small battery and electric start added with the engine swap, plus a master switch the baseline aircraft does not have. Creates a new failure mode the single-cylinder pull-start aircraft did not have: a flat battery on a Part 103 vehicle with no alternator.
Propeller re-pitched for the higher-power twin. Static RPM target differs from the baseline; the figure here is a placeholder.

airframe_specific.notes: Illustrative airframe. Registration is a placeholder and does not refer to a real aircraft.

derived_from.changes_summary: Engine swap from the Hirth F-33 single to the Kawasaki 340 twin, with electric start added. What that forced, in order of how much it matters: (1) Engine start is rewritten — the twin has two carburettors, so the choke behaviour differs and a carburettor synchronisation check was added to the preflight, which has no equivalent on the single. (2) A master switch and battery now exist, so they appear in the before-start and shutdown flows and in the engine-failure memory items; the baseline aircraft has no electrical system to isolate. (3) Static RPM in the before-takeoff run-up changed with the re-pitched propeller. (4) A new caution about battery state, because there is no alternator and a Part 103 vehicle has no required inspection to catch a tired battery. Everything else — airframe preflight, Part 103 limitations, engine failure after takeoff, shutdown discipline — is unchanged from the parent and was deliberately left alone so that a reader diffing the two files sees only the consequences of the swap.

source.notes: No manufacturer or engine manual was consulted. Forked from the project's own baseline Aerolite 103 file and edited to reflect a Kawasaki 340 installation. Airframe identification and the fact that both engines are published options come from the manufacturer's specification page; the procedures are the author's composition. Every RPM, temperature and voltage figure is a placeholder.

known_issues.description: No item has been checked against an aircraft or against the engine manufacturer's manual. Control and switch names may not match any real installation. Do not fly behind this file.
All RPM, temperature and electrical figures are placeholders, not limitations. Carburettor synchronisation and warm-up procedure must come from the Kawasaki manual for this engine.
Inherits the parent's gaps: no taxi, takeoff, cruise, descent or landing sections, and only one emergency procedure.

rights.notes: Forked from a CC-BY-4.0 file in this corpus; attribution to the parent is recorded in derived_from.

items.text: This aircraft is operated as an ultralight vehicle under 14 CFR Part 103. It has no airworthiness certificate and no N-number, and the pilot needs no certificate or medical.
Not over congested areas or open-air assemblies of people
Not in Class A, B, C or D airspace without prior ATC authorization
Part 103 imposes no maintenance or inspection requirement. Nobody else is checking this aircraft. The preflight is the entire inspection programme.

Weight check after the engine swap: the twin and the added battery are heavier than the single they replaced. Confirm the aircraft still meets the Part 103 empty weight limit, because exceeding it makes this an unregistered aircraft rather than an ultralight vehicle.
Wing struts, lift struts and attach bolts

items.response: NO TEARS, SEAMS INTACT, LACING SECURE

items.text: Control cables, pulleys and clevis pins

Treat the propeller as live at all times. A two-stroke can fire on a single blade movement with the ignition off if a switch or ground lead has failed. Keep the propeller arc clear and never stand in it.

items.response: NO NICKS OR CRACKS, TORQUE MARKS ALIGNED
LINKAGE FREE AND EVEN, SYNCHRONISATION MARKS ALIGNED
items.detail: New with the twin. An out-of-sync pair makes one cylinder work harder than the other, which on a two-stroke is a path to a holed piston. Not applicable to the single-cylinder baseline aircraft.
Confirm the premix ratio against the Kawasaki manual for this engine and oil. It is not necessarily the same ratio the previous engine used, and running a two-stroke on straight fuel will seize it.

items.text: There is no alternator. The battery starts the engine and is not recharged in flight. A battery that turned the engine over slowly today will not start it at a away-field, and nothing in Part 103 requires anyone to notice that before you go.

sections.title: Engine Start (Kawasaki 340, electric)
sections.notes: Rewritten from the parent: the twin's dual carburettors and the added electric start make the single-cylinder sequence inapplicable.

items.response: ON TOGETHER AS REQUIRED FOR TEMPERATURE
items.detail: Both must come on and off together. Choking one side only runs that cylinder rich and the other lean.

items.response: OFF PROGRESSIVELY AS ENGINE PICKS UP
PER ENGINE MANUAL BEFORE ADVANCING THROTTLE
items.detail: The twin takes longer to reach even temperature across both cylinders than the single did. A cold run-up is the classic path to a seizure.
A persistent split between cylinders points at a carburettor sync or air leak problem. Nothing on the baseline single-cylinder aircraft corresponds to this check.

items.response: PER ENGINE MANUAL FOR THIS PROPELLER PITCH
items.detail: Different from the baseline aircraft: both the engine and the propeller pitch changed. Establish the correct figure for this combination and placard it.
Decide before takeoff where the aircraft goes if the engine stops at 50 feet, at 200 feet, and at circuit height.

items.text: A two-stroke should be treated as an engine that will stop without warning. The twin is smoother than the single it replaced, which makes it easier to trust and no more likely to keep running. Do not depart over terrain that offers no landing option.

sections.title: Engine Failure After Takeoff
sections.condition: Engine stops or loses power after leaving the ground with insufficient height to return

items.text: Do not attempt to turn back to the runway. At this aircraft's altitude, speed and glide performance a turn back will stall it.

items.detail: Added with the electrical system. The baseline aircraft has no master switch to turn off.

items.text: Flare and land, accepting damage to the aircraft to protect the occupant

items.response: CONFIRM ENGINE STOPS WITH SWITCHES OFF
items.detail: If the engine continues to run with both switches off, the ignition ground has failed. Stop the engine with the fuel valve and do not fly again until the fault is found.
Added with the electrical system. Leaving it on flattens a battery that nothing recharges in flight.

items.text: Chock, tie down or hangar the aircraft
